justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline from what I assessed as the current price level near 970. For the one-day horizon, I placed the estimate at 971.5, essentially anchoring near the prevailing price with a very slight drift, since intraday momentum and short-term mean reversion tendencies tend to keep prices close to their recent anchor unless a catalyst emerges. For the one-week estimate of 975, I incorporated a small positive drift consistent with the general long-run upward bias in equity markets while acknowledging that a week is still a short enough window that noise dominates signal. The one-month estimate of 985 reflects a similar logic but with slightly more weight given to fundamental tailwinds such as earnings growth expectations and accommodative financial conditions, while still remaining humble about the limited magnitude of drift over just thirty days.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily to historical realized volatility at each horizon. Daily volatility in broad equity indices typically runs in the range of 0.8–1.2%, which translates to roughly plus or minus 8–12 points on a one-day basis, and I widened that to a 47-point range to account for fat tails and event risk. At the one-week horizon, volatility compounds roughly with the square root of time, justifying the wider 90-point range, and by one month the interval expands to 190 points reflecting the meaningful accumulation of uncertainty over that period. I also factored in that regime uncertainty — the possibility that volatility itself could shift — warranted slightly fatter tails than a simple Gaussian model would suggest.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data such as a worse-than-expected inflation print or employment report could trigger rapid repricing, as could a geopolitical shock or an unexpected central bank policy shift toward greater hawkishness. A credit event or liquidity disruption in financial markets could amplify selling pressure beyond normal volatility bounds. On the upside, a strongly positive earnings surprise season, a dovish pivot signal from a major central bank, or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical tension could propel prices well above the upper bound of my intervals, particularly at the one-month horizon where there is simply more time for large moves to accumulate.

It is worth emphasizing that probabilistic forecasts at these short horizons carry substantial inherent limitation. Markets are influenced by information flows that are by definition unknown at forecast time, and even well-calibrated intervals will be breached roughly 10% of the time by construction.
